summary: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM) are EU-funded master's programmes run by groups of universities in two or more countries; you study in at least two of them. Top-ranked applicants get a scholarship of EUR 1,400 a month for the whole programme (12–24 months), and the consortium covers tuition and insurance. Winners usually have strong grades, a clear reason for choosing that exact programme, and solid references.
lookfor: Academic record: degree class/GPA, relevance of your bachelor's to the programme
Motivation: why this specific programme, its modules and mobility track, and how it fits your career plan
Relevant experience: research, projects, work, publications, awards
Strength and specificity of reference letters
English level (and any other language the programme needs)
Each consortium sets and weights its own criteria — read the programme's selection rules
cycle: Each programme sets its own dates. For September 2027 entry most applications open October–November 2026 and close between about December 2026 and January 2027; interviews (if any) run January–March; scholarship results usually arrive March–April 2027, often with a reserve list.

eligibility.q: Do you hold a bachelor's degree, or will you finish it before the master's starts in 2027?
eligibility.no: Wait until you are in your final year. Use the time to build experience and save for English test fees.

eligibility.q: Have you never held an Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters scholarship before?
eligibility.no: Past EMJM scholarship holders cannot get another one. Look at DAAD EPOS, Swedish Institute, or university awards instead.

eligibility.q: Have you found at least one programme in the catalogue that matches your degree and offers scholarships for 2027 intake?
eligibility.no: Search the catalogue by field. Not every programme still has scholarship funding — check its website before investing time.

eligibility.q: Can you show English at the level the programme asks (often IELTS 6.5 or equivalent)?
eligibility.no: Book a test now. Some programmes accept proof that your degree was taught in English — ask the consortium in writing.

eligibility.q: Is your degree result strong (e.g. First Class or Second Class Upper, or the programme's stated minimum)?
eligibility.no: You can still apply, but pick programmes where your experience or research matches closely, and make your motivation letter and references very strong.

steps.title: Shortlist two or three programmes from the catalogue
steps.why: You apply to each programme separately, and selectors reward applicants whose background fits that exact programme.
do: Open the Erasmus Mundus Catalogue and filter by your field of study.
For each candidate programme, open its own website and find: entry requirements, scholarship availability for 2027, deadline, and document list.
Write these into a table: programme, universities/countries, deadline, English score needed, documents, number of references.
Cross out programmes that do not offer scholarships for 2027 or whose entry degree does not match yours.
Keep two or three programmes where your degree and experience fit best.
tips: Read the module list and mobility paths. You will need these details later for your motivation letter.

Look at the 'nationality' or 'geographical balance' notes: a consortium can give no more than 10% of its scholarships to one nationality, so very popular programmes are tight for big applicant countries like Nigeria.
avoid: Applying to many unrelated programmes with one generic letter.
Trusting a third-party list over the programme's own website.
check: I can name my 2–3 programmes, their deadlines and whether each offers scholarships for 2027.

steps.title: Understand what the scholarship pays and the rules
steps.why: Knowing the rules stops you wasting effort and helps you plan your budget and visa.
do: Read the Erasmus Mundus action in the Erasmus+ Programme Guide.
Note: EUR 1,400 per month for the full programme length; covers travel, visa, installation and living costs.
Note: tuition (participation costs) and insurance are handled by the consortium for scholarship holders — confirm on your programme's fees page.
Note: if you have held an EMJM scholarship before, you cannot get another.
tips: Many programmes also accept self-funded students. Decide now whether you would go without a scholarship.
avoid: Paying anyone who promises an Erasmus Mundus scholarship. EU scholarships are never granted for a fee.
check: I know what is covered and that I have never held an EMJM scholarship.

steps.title: Build your personal timeline
steps.why: You will juggle several deadlines, referees and a test date. A written plan prevents last-minute panic.
do: Write each programme's deadline in your calendar.
Set your own deadline three days earlier for each.
Work backwards: references requested 6–8 weeks before; English test at least 6 weeks before; transcripts 8 weeks before.
Put a weekly 2-hour block on your calendar for writing.
tips: Portals often slow down in the last 48 hours. Treat your own early deadline as the real one.
avoid: Planning around the earliest deadline only and forgetting the others.
check: Every deadline and every task has a date in my calendar.

steps.title: Create your account on each programme portal
steps.why: Each consortium has its own online form. Opening it early shows you every question and upload slot.
do: Go to each programme's 'Apply' page and register with an email you check daily.
Open every section of the form and copy the questions into a document.
List the exact files and formats asked for (PDF size limits, CV template, word limits).
Note how references are collected: upload by you, or emailed link to referee.
tips: Some programmes ask you to rank mobility tracks. Decide your preference using the module list.
avoid: Using a school or work email you may lose access to.
check: I have a list of every question and document for each programme.

steps.title: Request transcripts and degree certificate
steps.why: Missing or unofficial transcripts make an application ineligible.
do: Visit or email your university's Academic Office / Exams and Records unit and request official transcripts and a copy of your certificate.
Ask for an English version or certified translation if documents are not in English.
Scan the official copies in colour as clear PDFs.
If the programme wants certified copies, get them certified by your university or a notary, as the programme says.
tips: In Nigeria, transcript requests often take weeks and may need a fee paid at the bursary. Start now.
If you have not graduated yet, upload your latest transcript and a letter confirming expected graduation date.
check: I have clear PDFs of my transcript and certificate (or expected-graduation letter).

steps.title: Book and take your English test
steps.why: Most programmes reject applications without valid English proof.
do: Check each programme's accepted tests and minimum scores.
If you studied in English, ask the consortium in writing whether a Medium of Instruction letter is accepted.
If not, book IELTS Academic, TOEFL iBT or another listed test, leaving time for results before your earliest deadline.
Download the score report as PDF when it arrives.
tips: Ask your university for a Medium of Instruction letter anyway — some programmes accept it and it is cheap.
avoid: Booking a test whose results arrive after the deadline.
check: I have English proof accepted by every programme on my list.

steps.title: Prepare passport and CV
steps.why: Your CV is read first and frames everything else.
do: Check your passport is valid; renew it now if it expires before the end of 2028.
Write a CV in the format the programme asks (many ask for Europass); keep it to two pages unless told otherwise.
List education, research or final-year project, work, skills, awards and publications with dates.
Save as PDF named Surname_CV.pdf.
tips: Put your final-year project title and one line of results — selectors look for relevant academic work.
avoid: Long lists of duties without results.
check: My passport is valid and my CV is two pages in the required format.

steps.title: Write a motivation letter for each programme
steps.why: This is where most applicants are separated. Selectors want to see that you know their programme and have a clear plan.
do: Copy the programme's exact instructions and limit into the top of your draft.
Paragraph 1: the problem or field you care about and one concrete example from your experience.
Paragraph 2: what you have done so far — degree, project, work — with results.
Paragraph 3: why this programme: name modules, universities and the mobility track you want.
Paragraph 4: your career plan after graduation and how this degree gets you there.
Close with what you will add to the cohort.
Cut to the limit and save as PDF.
tips: Use different examples for each programme; do not just swap the name.
Specific beats general: 'I modelled flood risk for 12 villages in Benue' beats 'I am passionate about water'.
avoid: Opening with a quote or 'Since childhood I have...'.
Exceeding the page or word limit.
check: A stranger could tell which programme this letter is for without seeing the name.

steps.prompt: Set by each programme — usually why this programme, your background, and your career goals.
steps.limit: Set by each programme (often 1–2 pages or a word limit) — check the current guidance.

steps.title: Secure two or three strong referees
steps.why: Specific letters from people who know your work carry real weight in ranking.
do: Choose lecturers who supervised your project or taught you closely, plus an employer if you have work experience.
Ask each in person or by email at least 6–8 weeks before the deadline.
Send them: your CV, the programme description, the selection criteria, and 3–4 bullet points of things they saw you do.
Find out how the programme collects letters (you upload, or the portal emails them) and tell referees the date.
Remind them one week before your own deadline.
tips: If the portal sends links to referees, enter their details early — the link only goes out once you register them.
avoid: Asking a famous professor who barely knows you.
Writing the letter yourself for them to sign.
check: Every referee has agreed and knows the date and method.

steps.title: Fill the form and submit early
steps.why: Incomplete or late applications are not assessed.
do: Fill each section; copy essay answers from your checked document.
Upload each PDF to the correct slot and open it again to check it is the right file.
Confirm referees have submitted (if the portal shows status).
Read everything aloud once for typos.
Submit, then save or screenshot the confirmation page and email.
tips: Check the scholarship box if the form asks whether you want to be considered for the EMJM scholarship.
avoid: Forgetting to tick the scholarship consideration option.
check: I have a confirmation email for each application.

steps.title: Prepare for interviews or tests
steps.why: Some programmes shortlist candidates for an online interview or written task before final ranking.
do: Check your email (and spam) daily after the deadline.
If invited, reply quickly and confirm the time zone.
Prepare 2-minute answers: why this programme, your project, your career plan, which mobility track and why.
Test your internet, camera and a quiet room; have a backup data plan.
tips: Re-read your own motivation letter — interviewers often ask about it.
avoid: Missing an invitation because it went to spam.
check: I can explain my fit for the programme in two minutes.

steps.title: Respond to results and start the visa
steps.why: Offers have reply deadlines; reserve-list candidates often get scholarships when others decline.
do: Read your result: main list, reserve list, self-funded offer, or rejection.
Accept within the deadline if you want the place; decline others promptly so places move to reserves.
Follow the consortium's instructions for the visa of your first country and book an appointment early.
If unsuccessful, ask for feedback and plan for the next round, which usually opens in October.
tips: If you are on a reserve list, keep checking email into May or June.
avoid: Holding several offers until the last minute.
check: I have accepted one offer in writing and know my visa steps.

faq.q: Do I apply to the EU or to the programme?
faq.a: To the programme. Each consortium runs its own application and selects scholarship holders.

faq.q: How many programmes can I apply to?
faq.a: Each programme is a separate application. Apply only to those that really fit you; check each programme's own rules.

faq.q: Is there tuition to pay if I win?
faq.a: Scholarship holders do not pay participation costs; confirm details on your programme's fees page.
The EU rules do not set one; check your programme's page.

faq.q: Someone is offering to secure me a place for a fee. Is this real?
faq.a: No. EU scholarships are never granted for a fee.
